nodes.label: Directed Line Segments and Geometric Vectors
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background in planar Euclidean geometry (lengths, parallel lines, triangles, and parallelograms) and basic algebra. Introduces vectors as quantities with both magnitude and direction in contrast to scalars, representing them geometrically as directed line segments (arrows) from an initial point (tail) to a terminal point (head). Establishes equivalence of free vectors under parallel translation—two directed segments represent the same vector if and only if they have the same length and direction, regardless of location—together with the zero vector 0 (length zero, undefined direction) and the opposite vector −v (same length, reversed direction). Develops geometric vector addition via both the head-to-tail (triangle) rule and the parallelogram rule, geometric subtraction as u − v = u + (−v) (linking the tail-to-tail arrow from v's head to u's head to displacement), and geometric scalar multiplication kv (scaling length by |k| and reversing direction when k < 0). Justifies commutativity, associativity, and geometric parallelism (nonzero vectors are parallel iff one is a scalar multiple of the other) from triangle and parallelogram constructions, addressing common errors such as treating translated copies as different vectors or reversing the arrow of u − v. Enables the learner to sketch sums, differences, and scalar multiples of planar vectors, interpret multi-leg displacements geometrically, and test geometric parallelism. Leaves Cartesian coordinates, component arithmetic, trigonometry, and 3D space to subsequent lessons and trees.

nodes.label: Component Form, Position Vectors, and Standard Basis
nodes.explanation: Builds on geometric vectors, assuming familiarity with the 2D Cartesian coordinate plane and basic linear algebra operations on real numbers, to bridge arrow geometry and coordinate algebra. Translates any free vector to standard position with its tail at the origin to define its position vector and Cartesian component form v = ⟨v_x, v_y⟩, deriving the displacement formula PQ→ = ⟨x_Q − x_P, y_Q − y_P⟩ (emphasizing terminal minus initial coordinates and showing that parallel translation leaves components unchanged). Introduces the standard unit basis vectors i = ⟨1, 0⟩ and j = ⟨0, 1⟩ and the equivalent linear-combination representation v = v_x i + v_y j. Uses right triangles and similar triangles as the geometric bridge from head-to-tail addition and geometric scaling to the exact componentwise rules ⟨u_x, u_y⟩ ± ⟨v_x, v_y⟩ = ⟨u_x ± v_x, u_y ± v_y⟩ and k⟨v_x, v_y⟩ = ⟨kv_x, kv_y⟩, verifying the algebraic laws of vector arithmetic (commutativity, associativity, distributivity, and additive inverses) and solving linear vector equations such as 2u + 3x = v for an unknown vector x. Enables the learner to convert fluently among geometric segments, endpoint coordinates, component form, and i, j notation, and compute exact algebraic combinations of planar vectors. Leaves lengths, unit vectors, direction angles, and dot products to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Magnitude, Unit Vectors, and Algebraic Parallelism
nodes.explanation: Builds on component form and vector arithmetic, assuming the Pythagorean theorem and basic square-root manipulation, to quantify vector lengths and pure directions in ℝ². Defines the Euclidean magnitude (norm) ‖v‖ = √(v_x² + v_y²) directly from the right triangle of components, proving ‖v‖ ≥ 0 with ‖v‖ = 0 iff v = 0, the scaling identity ‖kv‖ = |k|‖v‖ (explicitly highlighting the absolute value |k| when k < 0 to prevent sign errors), and the geometric triangle inequality ‖u + v‖ ≤ ‖u‖ + ‖v‖ (identifying equality with same-direction alignment). Defines unit vectors (‖û‖ = 1), develops normalization û = v / ‖v‖ for any nonzero v, and trains constructing a vector of prescribed length L in the same or opposite direction as a given vector (±L v / ‖v‖). Establishes the algebraic test for parallel vectors (u = kv for some scalar k, equivalently the zero cross-difference u_x v_y − u_y v_x = 0, handled cleanly even when a component is zero) and applies it to test whether three coordinate points are collinear. Enables the learner to compute lengths and distances, normalize vectors, scale directions to target magnitudes, and verify parallelism or collinearity algebraically. Leaves trigonometric direction angles and dot products to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Position Vectors, Section Formula, and 2D Geometric Proofs
nodes.explanation: Builds on component form and position vectors (staying within affine vector combinations without needing lengths or angles) to apply vectors to planar coordinate-free geometry. Represents points by position vectors r_P = OP→ and derives the internal section formula r_P = (n r_A + m r_B)/(m + n) = (1 − t)r_A + t r_B (t = m/(m + n) ∈ [0, 1]) for a point dividing segment AB in the ratio m : n, specializing to the midpoint (r_A + r_B)/2 and the triangle centroid (r_A + r_B + r_C)/3. Introduces the vector and parametric equations of a 2D line r(t) = r_0 + t d (connecting a nonzero direction vector d = ⟨d_x, d_y⟩ to slope d_y / d_x when d_x ≠ 0 while treating vertical lines without special cases) and tests point-on-line membership and intersection of two parametric lines via 2×2 linear systems. Trains coordinate-free vector proofs of classic planar theorems by expressing geometric conditions as vector identities—such as showing the segment joining midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to and half the third side, diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, and medians of a triangle are concurrent at the centroid. Enables the learner to compute division points and centroids, write and intersect parametric 2D lines, and construct rigorous planar geometric proofs using position vectors. Leaves perpendicularity, angles, and point-to-line distances to dot-product lessons, and 3D lines to analytic geometry in space.

nodes.label: Direction Angles, Polar Form, and Vector Resolution
nodes.explanation: Builds on vector magnitude and unit vectors, assuming secondary trigonometry (sine, cosine, and tangent on the unit circle, reference angles across all four quadrants, and inverse tangent), to connect component form with magnitude–direction form. Defines the standard direction angle θ ∈ [0°, 360°) (or [0, 2π)) measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis, deriving component resolution v = ‖v‖⟨cos θ, sin θ⟩ = (‖v‖ cos θ)i + (‖v‖ sin θ)j and identifying ⟨cos θ, sin θ⟩ as the unit vector in direction θ. Develops the inverse conversion from components ⟨v_x, v_y⟩ to (‖v‖, θ) using tan θ = v_y / v_x paired with mandatory quadrant inspection—explicitly guarding against the pervasive misconception that arctan(v_y / v_x) alone gives the direction angle in Quadrants II and III—and handles axis-aligned vectors where v_x = 0 directly. Bridges standard mathematical direction angles to compass bearings (clockwise from North) and navigation headings, and trains summing several angled vectors by resolving each into x- and y-components, summing components, and converting the resultant back to magnitude and direction. Enables the learner to convert accurately between rectangular and magnitude–direction forms in every quadrant and resolve angled planar vectors for resultant calculations. Leaves projections onto arbitrary non-axis directions to the dot-product branch and physical modeling to application lessons.

nodes.label: The 2D Dot Product and Angles Between Vectors
nodes.explanation: Builds on vector magnitude and component arithmetic, assuming the Law of Cosines from secondary trigonometry, to develop the 2D dot (scalar) product and angle measurement between arbitrary vectors. Defines the algebraic dot product u · v = u_x v_x + u_y v_y, stressing that its output is a scalar rather than a vector, and verifies its algebraic laws: commutativity (u · v = v · u), distributivity over vector addition, scalar homogeneity ((ku) · v = k(u · v)), and the norm identity v · v = ‖v‖². Establishes the geometric formula u · v = ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ (for the angle θ ∈ [0, π] between nonzero u and v) by applying the Law of Cosines to the triangle formed by u, v, and u − v and expanding ‖u − v‖² = (u − v) · (u − v). Extracts the angle formula cos θ = (u · v)/(‖u‖ ‖v‖), interprets the sign of u · v geometrically (positive ↔ acute, zero ↔ right angle, negative ↔ obtuse), and notes the 2D Cauchy–Schwarz inequality |u · v| ≤ ‖u‖ ‖v‖ directly from |cos θ| ≤ 1. Enables the learner to compute dot products in algebraic or geometric form, determine exact or approximate angles between planar vectors without first finding axis direction angles, and classify angle types from component data. Leaves perpendicular constructions, normal line equations, projections, and 3D dot products to subsequent lessons and trees.

nodes.label: Orthogonality, Perpendicular Vectors, and Normal Form of a Line
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes the 2D dot product and parametric planar lines to handle perpendicularity and dual descriptions of lines in ℝ². Establishes the algebraic orthogonality test u · v = 0 (distinguishing perpendicular nonzero vectors from the convention that 0 is orthogonal to every vector) and derives the 2D 90°-rotation construction sending ⟨a, b⟩ to the orthogonal pair ⟨−b, a⟩ and ⟨b, −a⟩, linking perpendicularity to the slope relation m_1 m_2 = −1 while seamlessly including horizontal and vertical lines. Develops the point-normal equation of a 2D line n · (r − r_0) = 0, expanding it to Cartesian form ax + by = c where n = ⟨a, b⟩ is perpendicular to the line, and trains converting fluently between parametric form r_0 + t d and normal/Cartesian form. Computes acute angles between intersecting lines via either direction vectors or normal vectors (using |u · v| to select the acute angle), and applies the dot product to coordinate-free right-angle geometric proofs—such as proving Thales' theorem (an angle inscribed in a semicircle is 90° via (p − a) · (p + a) = ‖p‖² − ‖a‖² = 0) and that diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular. Enables the learner to construct orthogonal vectors, switch effortlessly between parametric and normal equations of planar lines, and prove planar perpendicularity theorems via dot products. Leaves projections and point-to-line distances to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Scalar and Vector Projections and Orthogonal Decomposition
nodes.explanation: Builds on the 2D dot product to generalize horizontal/vertical resolution to arbitrary nonzero reference directions. Derives the signed scalar projection (component of u along v) comp_v u = (u · v)/‖v‖ = ‖u‖ cos θ, interpreting its sign as alignment with or opposition to v, and defines the vector projection proj_v u = (comp_v u)(v / ‖v‖) = ((u · v)/(v · v)) v. Explicitly addresses the two most frequent errors: dividing by ‖v‖ instead of ‖v‖² in the vector projection formula, and confusing proj_v u (which lies along v) with proj_u v (which lies along u). Establishes the orthogonal decomposition of any planar vector u relative to a nonzero direction v as u = u_∥ + u_⊥ where u_∥ = proj_v u and u_⊥ = u − proj_v u, proving algebraically that u_∥ · u_⊥ = 0 and verifying the Pythagorean length relation ‖u‖² = ‖u_∥‖² + ‖u_⊥‖². Enables the learner to compute scalar and vector projections along any specified 2D vector and decompose planar vectors into parallel and perpendicular parts. Leaves point-to-line distances and physical work/inclined-plane applications to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Point-to-Line Distance and Orthogonal Projections onto Lines
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes normal line equations and orthogonal vector projections to solve metric problems involving points and lines in ℝ². Given a line L in normal form n · (r − r_0) = 0 (ax + by = c) and an external point P, constructs the orthogonal projection of the displacement r_P − r_0 onto the normal vector n to locate the closest point (foot of the perpendicular) F = r_P − proj_n(r_P − r_0) on L, and also shows the equivalent construction along a direction vector d when L is given parametrically as r_0 + t d. Derives the exact shortest distance formula d(P, L) = |comp_n(r_P − r_0)| = |n · (r_P − r_0)| / ‖n‖ = |ax_P + by_P − c| / √(a² + b²) and specializes it to the distance between two parallel lines. Extends the foot construction to compute the mirror reflection of P across L via r_P' = r_P − 2 proj_n(r_P − r_0), checking visually and algebraically that the midpoint of PP' lies on L and PP' ⊥ L. Enables the learner to compute exact point-to-line distances, closest points, and planar reflections across arbitrary lines using vector projections. Leaves 3D point-to-plane, point-to-line, and skew-line distances to Vectors and Analytic Geometry in Space.

nodes.label: Resultant Forces and 2D Static Equilibrium
nodes.explanation: Builds on direction angles and vector resolution, assuming familiarity with solving 2×2 linear systems and basic physical notions of force magnitude and downward weight (supplying Newton's first-law equilibrium condition ∑ F = 0 as a modeling premise without requiring a prior physics course), to apply planar vectors to statics. Models concurrent forces acting at a point as 2D vectors, computes the resultant (net) force F_net = ∑ F_i by resolving each force into horizontal and vertical components and recombining into magnitude and direction, and defines the equilibrant −F_net needed to restore balance. Formulates 2D static equilibrium as the component system ∑ F_x = 0 and ∑ F_y = 0, guiding the learner through drawing clean force diagrams, choosing convenient coordinate axes (including axes rotated parallel and perpendicular to an inclined plane), and solving multi-force equilibrium systems—such as a suspended weight supported by two cables at unequal angles (solving for unknown tensions) and a block held at rest on a smooth ramp. Enables the learner to translate planar force scenarios into vector equations, determine resultants and equilibrants, and solve for unknown force magnitudes and angles in static equilibrium. Leaves mechanical work to the projection-based work lesson and 3D forces/torques to analytic geometry in space.

nodes.label: Relative Velocity and Planar Navigation Problems
nodes.explanation: Builds on direction angles and vector resolution to model planar velocities in moving media and relative motion between moving objects. Represents velocity as a 2D vector whose magnitude is speed and whose direction is the course or heading, reinforcing careful conversion between compass bearings (clockwise from North, e.g. N 30° E or 120°) and standard mathematical angles. Develops velocity composition v_ground = v_craft + v_medium (such as aircraft velocity relative to air plus wind velocity, or boat velocity relative to water plus river current) and relative velocity v_{A/B} = v_A − v_B, sharply distinguishing intended heading (pointing direction) from true ground track (actual path). Trains both forward calculations (finding ground speed and actual track from heading and wind/current) and inverse drift-correction calculations (determining the required heading angle and ground speed to follow a prescribed course across a crosswind or current, including recognizing when no solution exists because the cross-component of the current exceeds the craft's maximum speed). Enables the learner to set up and solve planar navigation, current-crossing, and relative-velocity problems accurately. Leaves variable velocities, curves, and acceleration derivatives to calculus.

nodes.label: Work Done by a Constant Force and Tilted-Axis Analysis
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes orthogonal vector projections and 2D force modeling to compute mechanical work and resolve forces along arbitrary tilted directions without manually rotating coordinate frames. Defines the work done by a constant planar force F acting across a straight displacement d as W = F · d = (comp_d F) ‖d‖ = ‖F‖ ‖d‖ cos θ, interpreting positive work (force aids motion), zero work (force perpendicular to displacement, such as a normal force on a track), and negative work (opposing force such as friction or braking). Uses distributivity of the dot product to establish that the work done by the resultant force equals the algebraic sum of the works done by individual forces ((∑ F_i) · d = ∑ (F_i · d)). Applies scalar and vector projections directly to split gravity or an angled pulling force into components parallel and normal to a ramp given by a direction vector or slope, linking projection formulas seamlessly to physical force components and work calculations. Enables the learner to compute work from either component or angle-magnitude data, interpret the sign of work physically, and decompose planar forces along tilted lines via orthogonal projection. Leaves work by variable forces along curved paths (line integrals) to multivariable calculus.

nodes.label: Linear Combinations and Non-Standard 2D Bases
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on vector components, scaling, and algebraic parallelism (assuming fluency with solving 2×2 linear systems) to introduce linear combinations and planar bases as a bridge toward linear algebra. Defines a linear combination c_1 u + c_2 v of two planar vectors and interprets it geometrically as navigating a skewed parallelogram grid spanned by u and v. Proves algebraically that any target vector w ∈ ℝ² can be written uniquely as w = c_1 u + c_2 v if and only if u and v are non-parallel (equivalently u_x v_y − u_y v_x ≠ 0), contrasting this unique-representation property (a basis of ℝ²) with parallel (linearly dependent) pairs whose linear combinations collapse onto a single line (yielding either no solution or infinitely many solutions). Trains expressing a given vector in an oblique 2D basis—such as resolving a required resultant force along two non-perpendicular cables—and verifying the coordinates by direct recombination. Enables the learner to test whether two planar vectors span ℝ² uniquely and compute coordinates relative to non-standard 2D bases. Leaves general ℝ^n vector spaces, matrices, and formal linear independence proofs to Linear Algebra.
